target.title: Whisper-Flamingo: Integrating Visual Features into Whisper for Audio-Visual Speech Recognition and Translation
target.version: Interspeech 2024 proceedings, pp. 2420-2424 (same tables as arXiv:2406.10082v1, 2024-06); arXiv:2406.10082v3 (2024-11-19) consulted for the authors' revised Table 3 and Appendix

entries.text: Novel Whisper-Flamingo inserts AV-HuBERT visual features into Whisper's decoder through gated cross-attention.
entries.condition: Audio-visual speech recognition and speech translation; gated cross-attention layers attend to AV-HuBERT visual features.
entries.quote: Inspired by this method, we propose Whisper-Flamingo which inserts gated cross attention layers into Whisper’s decoder and enables Whisper to use lip-based features for speech recognition.

entries.text: The Whisper audio model was pretrained using 680k hours of speech.
entries.condition: Audio-only Whisper pretraining; described as the base model for visual-feature adaptation.

entries.text: The authors claim both the video model and text decoder are pretrained on large-scale data, unlike prior audio-visual adaptations that train these components from scratch on a few hundred video hours.
entries.condition: Comparison with prior audio-visual adaptation methods [5-7].

entries.text: The authors present audio-visual speech translation as a task not explored by the prior audio-only adaptation methods they cite.
entries.condition: Prior methods [5-7] are the stated comparison set.

entries.text: One Whisper-Flamingo parameter set performs English transcription and En-X translation, whereas prior methods are trained separately by language.
entries.condition: English transcription plus translation into the six MuAViC target languages.
entries.quote: Our model performs both En speech recognition and En-X speech translation using one set of parameters while previous methods fine-tune separately on each language.

entries.text: The En-X translation task covers six target languages: Greek, Spanish, French, Italian, Portuguese, and Russian.
entries.condition: English audio to text in El, Es, Fr, It, Pt, and Ru using MuAViC.
entries.quote:
Our model performs En tran-
scription and En-X translation into 6 other languages, while the previous audio-visual SOTA requires fine-tuning on each language separately.

entries.text: The authors describe the decoder fusion method as a generic way to insert a visual encoder into an ASR decoder and suggest it could transfer to models trained on more data.
entries.condition: Forward-looking conclusion; not validated with a second audio model in this paper.

entries.text: Training proceeds by fine-tuning all audio-only Whisper parameters first, then freezing the adapted Whisper and training the new gated cross-attention and visual projection layers from scratch.
entries.condition: Whisper-Flamingo audio-visual training; AV-HuBERT weights are frozen, with dropout and batch-normalization updating enabled as specified in Sec. 3.1.
entries.quote:
To train Whisper-Flamingo, we freeze the fine-tuned Whisper, in-
sert the gated cross attention layers, and fine-tune the model
with audio-visual inputs.

entries.text: The training objective is cross-entropy between predicted transcript tokens and ground-truth tokens.
entries.condition: Audio-only Whisper fine-tuning and audio-visual Whisper-Flamingo fine-tuning.

entries.text: Training noise is sampled at 0-SNR from MUSAN natural, music, and babble noise, plus overlapping speech sampled from LRS3.
entries.condition: Noise augmentation during training; sampled noise sources are MUSAN and LRS3 speech.
entries.quote: During training, we randomly add noise to the audio with a signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of 0.

entries.text: LRS3 English data is divided into 433 hours of training data, one hour of validation data, and one hour of test data.
entries.condition: LRS3 English TED-talk video dataset; split procedure follows AV-HuBERT [4].

entries.text: Video is 25-fps grayscale; Dlib extracts 96x96 lip crops aligned to a reference mean face, with random 88x88 training crops and center 88x88 test crops.
entries.condition: Video sensing and crop protocol; horizontal training flip probability is 0.5.

entries.text: Audio input uses 80-bin log-Mel features from 16-kHz audio, with a 25-ms window and 10-ms stride.
entries.unit: Mel bins; kHz; ms window; ms stride
entries.condition: Whisper audio front-end for the experiments.

entries.text: The visual encoder is AV-HuBERT Large with 325M parameters; Whisper-Large gated cross-attention adds 630M parameters, yielding a 2.5B-parameter complete model and 631M trainable parameters.
entries.unit: parameters: AV-HuBERT; gated cross-attention; total; trainable
entries.condition: Whisper-Large audio-visual model, including AV-HuBERT; AV-HuBERT and base Whisper weights are otherwise frozen during the AV stage.
entries.quote:
For Whisper Large, the gated cross atten-
tion layers add 630M parameters, bringing the total number
of parameters to 2.5B (including AV-HuBERT).

entries.text: Whisper Small, Medium, and Large-v2 contain 244M, 769M, and 1.55B parameters, respectively.
entries.condition: Audio model size used in the experiments.

entries.text: Table 1 reports audio-only Whisper-Large fine-tuning at 90k steps on one GPU for En recognition and 225k steps on four GPUs for En-X; Whisper-Flamingo uses 20k steps on one GPU for En recognition and 40k steps on four GPUs for En-X.
entries.unit: training steps: Whisper FT En / FT En-X / Flamingo En / Flamingo En-X
entries.condition: Table 1 settings; Whisper-FT warmup is 1k steps, Whisper-Flamingo warmup is 5k steps; respective learning rates are 5e-6 and 1e-4.

entries.text: Best checkpoints are selected by highest token prediction accuracy on noisy validation data, monitored every 1k steps.
entries.condition: Noisy validation set; selection metric is token prediction accuracy.

entries.text: Reported decoding uses beam search with beam size 15; WER uses Fairseq normalization and BLEU uses SacreBLEU's default 13-a tokenizer.
entries.condition: WER: remove punctuation and lowercase before scoring; translation: SacreBLEU default 13-a tokenizer.
entries.quote: We report beam search decoding results with beam size 15.

entries.text: LRS3 clean WER is measured on the original test set; noisy WER uses babble noise added at 0-SNR.
entries.condition: English transcription, LRS3 test set, original clean audio versus babble-noise audio.
entries.quote: We report results on the original test set (Clean) and with babble noise injected at 0-SNR (Noisy).

entries.text: Whisper Medium zero-shot obtains 2.3% clean WER and 22.2% noisy WER in the LRS3 fusion ablation.
entries.condition: LRS3 original test set; Whisper-Medium audio-only zero-shot, no fine-tuning.
entries.quote: Whisper, Zero-shot A 2.3 22.2

entries.condition: Whisper-Medium with AV-HuBERT 25-Hz features duplicated to 50 Hz and added before the audio encoder; LRS3 test set.
entries.quote: Whisper-Early-Fusion AV 1.7 10.0

entries.text: Whisper-Flamingo obtains 1.5% clean WER and 7.0% noisy WER, the best noisy result in the Whisper-Medium fusion ablation.
entries.condition: Whisper-Medium audio-visual model on LRS3; gated cross-attention fusion.
entries.quote: Whisper-Flamingo AV 1.5 7.0

entries.text: The authors say gated cross-attention performs better than early and late fusion, and that freezing Whisper helps retain its audio skills while the new layers integrate video.
entries.condition: Whisper-Medium LRS3 ablation; insertion order was also tested, with other orders reported as slightly worse.
entries.quote:
Freezing Whisper helps retain its strong audio skills while new cross attention lay-
ers enable it to integrate the visual modality more effectively.

entries.condition: LRS3 English transcription test; 0-SNR babble condition; audio-only fine-tuned Whisper-Large versus Whisper-Flamingo Large.

entries.condition: Prior AV-HuBERT SSL result; uses a different LRS3 babble-noise file from the target method.

entries.text: u-HuBERT reports the best noisy LRS3 WER in the comparison, 4.6%, and 1.3% clean WER.
entries.condition: Prior u-HuBERT result; uses a different LRS3 babble-noise file and its model weights were unavailable to the authors.
entries.quote:
The best noisy performance (4.6%)

entries.text: FAVA-USM reports 1.3% clean and 6.2% noisy WER, with 12M hours of audio-only unlabeled pretraining and 5000 labeled hours.
entries.unit: % WER, clean / noisy; unlabeled audio hours; labeled audio hours
entries.condition: Prior FAVA-USM system on LRS3; AV labeled hours are 433; noisy comparison uses a different noise dataset.

entries.text: Adaptive AV reports 2.3% clean and 16.3% noisy WER; FAVA reports 1.7% clean and 6.6% noisy WER.
entries.unit: % WER, clean / noisy; Adaptive AV / FAVA
entries.condition: Prior audio-only-pretrain plus audio-visual-fine-tune systems on LRS3; their noisy scores use different noise sets.

entries.text: The authors caution that direct noisy comparisons are difficult because systems used different noise datasets; the AV-HuBERT/u-HuBERT noise files were unavailable and the recreated conditions are only similar, not identical.
entries.condition: LRS3 noisy WER comparisons in Table 3.
entries.quote:
Direct comparison in noisy conditions is challenging since dif-
ferent noise datasets were used to generate the babble noise.

entries.text: The authors claim Whisper-Flamingo is competitive with AV-HuBERT on clean LRS3 WER and slightly better on noisy WER, while outperforming audio-only adaptation approaches in noise; they qualify noisy comparisons as not strictly comparable.
entries.condition: Table 3 LRS3 results; differing babble-noise sources limit cross-system comparisons.

entries.text: For clean En-X translation, fine-tuned Whisper-Large averages 22.7 BLEU, versus 21.9 for Bilingual AV-HuBERT.
entries.condition: Clean audio, MuAViC English audio translated into six target languages; the prior Bilingual AV-HuBERT uses language-specific fine-tuning.
entries.quote: Testing with clean audio, we achieve an average BLEU score of 22.7, which outperforms the previous SOTA of 21.9 from Bilingual AV-HuBERT.

entries.text: Text-to-text systems using ground-truth English text score 23.1 BLEU for M2M-100 and 24.3 for the bilingual Transformer.
entries.unit: average BLEU, multilingual / bilingual text-to-text systems
entries.condition: Machine translation from ground-truth English text, not speech translation; Table 4 upper rows.

entries.text: On clean MuAViC audio, Whisper-Flamingo Large scores 1.3% English WER and BLEU 24.4, 27.9, 25.9, 22.1, 21.8, and 15.7 for El, Es, Fr, It, Pt, and Ru, averaging 22.9.
entries.unit: % WER; BLEU by El / Es / Fr / It / Pt / Ru / average
entries.condition: Clean speech-to-text translation on MuAViC; audio-visual Whisper-Flamingo Large, one model for all target languages.

entries.unit: % WER; BLEU by El / Es / Fr / It / Pt / Ru / average
entries.condition: Clean speech-to-text translation on MuAViC; audio-only Whisper-Large fine-tuned for En-X.

entries.condition: Prior Bilingual AV-HuBERT speech-to-text translation, clean audio; separately fine-tuned per language pair.

entries.condition: Comparison uses Table 4 clean MuAViC results; text-to-text baselines receive ground-truth English text.

entries.text: In the paper's noisy MuAViC comparison, Whisper-Flamingo improves over audio-only Whisper-Large from 18.6 to 20.5 average BLEU and from 13.8% to 7.2% English WER.
entries.condition: Noisy En-X speech-to-text translation; MuAViC multilingual babble condition.
entries.quote:
With multilingual babble noise, Whisper-Flamingo significantly outperforms the audio-
only Whisper model in average BLEU score (20.5 vs 18.6)
and En WER (7.2% vs 13.8%).

entries.text: On noisy MuAViC translation, Bilingual AV-HuBERT averages 15.0 BLEU audio-only and 20.8 BLEU audio-visually.
entries.condition: Prior Bilingual AV-HuBERT on noisy MuAViC; its babble-noise file differs from the target method's file.

entries.text: The authors acknowledge Whisper-Flamingo's noisy average BLEU is slightly below Bilingual AV-HuBERT's (20.5 versus 20.8), although one model handles both English transcription and all translation directions.
entries.condition: Noisy MuAViC translation; separate prior language-specific models versus one multilingual model.
entries.quote: our audio-visual performance is slightly worse (20.5 vs 20.8).

entries.text: The En-X noisy test condition is made by mixing speech from nine languages and 30 speakers; the authors note the comparison noise file was not publicly available and their conditions are similar but not identical.
entries.condition: Multilingual babble used for MuAViC noisy speech translation; distinct from the English LRS3 babble test.

entries.text: Whisper-Flamingo performs English transcription and En-X translation with one model, while Bilingual AV-HuBERT fine-tunes separately for each language pair and trains decoders from scratch.
entries.condition: MuAViC En-X translation to six languages plus English transcription.
entries.quote:
our models perform both En-X translation and En transcription with a single
model, while their models fine-tune separately for each lan-
guage pair.

entries.text: Across Small, Medium, and Large models, Whisper-Flamingo scores better than audio-only Whisper in noisy MuAViC conditions, and the authors report performance generally improves with model size.
entries.unit: % En WER and average BLEU, Small / Medium / Large
entries.condition: Noisy MuAViC En-X; corresponding audio-only WER is 17.3 / 14.8 / 13.8 and average BLEU 16.7 / 17.6 / 18.6.
entries.quote: Whisper-Flamingo always does better in noise compared to the audio-only baselines, and performance tends to improve as the model size increases.

entries.text: The authors tried multilingual recognition and X-En translation but did not pursue them: most languages had less than one-third of English training hours, while longer videos increased memory use and forced smaller batches.
entries.unit: of English data hours (threshold described qualitatively)
entries.condition: MuAViC multilingual speech recognition and X-En translation experiments; these tasks are deferred to future work.

entries.text: The authors could not test Whisper-Flamingo with u-HuBERT features because u-HuBERT weights were unavailable, even though u-HuBERT had the strongest noisy LRS3 score in their comparison.
entries.condition: LRS3 visual-encoder comparison; u-HuBERT's reported noisy WER is 4.6%.
entries.quote:
we would like to try it as a visual encoder for Whisper-Flamingo, but the weights are not publicly
available.

entries.text: The paper does not report random seeds, repeated runs, confidence intervals, or a statistical test for its use of 'significantly'; the numerical comparisons therefore have no reported variability estimate.
entries.condition: All WER and BLEU comparisons, including claims described as significant.
entries.quote: Our audio-visual Whisper-Flamingo significantly outperforms audio-only Whisper in noise.

entries.text: The paper gives LRS3 split durations but does not state whether speakers, talk sessions, or source videos overlap across train, validation, and test partitions.
entries.condition: LRS3 433-hour train, one-hour validation, and one-hour test split.

entries.text: No chance-level comparator is reported; the paper reports WER and BLEU rather than a chance-based classification metric.
entries.condition: All reported speech-recognition and translation evaluations.

entries.text: The linked training and decoding scripts set the random seed to 3407; the repository scripts show one configured seed and no repeated-seed evaluation loop.
entries.condition: Training and decoding; setting a seed does not by itself establish deterministic execution.
entries.quote: We used A6000 GPUs with 48GB memory.

entries.text: The training scripts pass reduce_val=200 for En-X, which caps the validation lists (and, through the operator precedence in utils.py, the test lists loaded during training) at 200 examples per language; the decoding script calls load_data without reduce_val, so the test sets used for reported decoding are not capped.
entries.condition: Training-time monitoring versus decoding; whisper_decode_video.py:61 calls load_data without reduce_val; utils.py:271 reads `if split == 'valid' or split == 'test' and reduce_val is not None`.

entries.text: The repository scales video pixels by 255 and then normalizes using mean 0.421 and standard deviation 0.165 for both training and testing.
entries.unit: pixel mean / standard deviation after scaling to 0-1
entries.condition: Training uses random crop and 0.5 horizontal flip; testing uses center crop; paper reports the crop and flip but not pixel normalization.

entries.text: The code converts 16-bit waveform samples to float by dividing by 32768 before log-Mel feature extraction; this amplitude scaling is not stated in the paper.
entries.condition: Audio-only and audio-visual dataset paths; audio is then passed to Whisper log-Mel extraction.

entries.text: The repository README says non-English MuAViC labels have punctuation removed except single apostrophes, with the normalization applied to training, validation, and test text; the paper does not specify this label preprocessing.
entries.condition: MuAViC non-English En-X translation labels; all data splits are normalized.

entries.text: The repository's noise-preparation README specifies multilingual babble construction from 30 speakers with at least 15 seconds of audio each and at least three speakers per language; the paper reports nine languages and 30 speakers but omits these selection thresholds.
entries.unit: speakers; minimum audio seconds; minimum speakers per language
entries.condition: MuAViC multilingual babble noise for En-X noisy evaluation.

entries.text: The audio-visual training config sets noise_prob=1.0, so noise is added to every training sample in that configuration; the paper describes random noise addition but not this probability.
entries.condition: Audio-visual En-X config; noise_snr_train is 0 and the noise list points to MUSAN training noise.

entries.text: During audio-visual training, the script includes noisy and clean test dataloaders in the validation loop before fitting and in subsequent fit-time validation calls; the checkpoint monitor is still the noisy validation metric.
entries.condition: Evaluation protocol exposure: test metrics are computed during training; paper describes noisy-validation checkpoint selection but does not mention these test-dataloader calls.

entries.text: The loader filters training examples by configured maximum audio length, limits validation audio to 30 seconds, and does not apply the same duration filter to test examples; this split-specific filtering is not fully described in the paper.
entries.unit: seconds, configured training maximum / validation maximum
entries.condition: For the En-X audio config, audio_max_length is 160000 samples (10 seconds); test examples are not filtered by duration in load_data.

entries.text: The English LRS3 noisy comparison with AV-HuBERT and u-HuBERT is not identical because their original generated noise file was unavailable; the MuAViC noisy comparison similarly uses a non-public comparator noise file.
entries.condition: Cross-paper noisy WER and BLEU comparisons.
entries.quote:
that their noise file was not publicly available, so our noisy con-
ditions are similar but not identical.

entries.text: The paper does not report the number of MuAViC test utterances or the test-set duration for each En-X language; the decoding script loads the full test split (no reduce_val).
entries.condition: MuAViC translation test evaluation for El, Es, Fr, It, Pt, and Ru.
entries.quote:
Our model performs En tran-
scription and En-X translation into 6 other languages, while the previous audio-visual SOTA requires fine-tuning on each language separately.

entries.text: The authors state that most methods adapting pre-trained audio-only models to AVSR use early fusion; FAVA adapts BEST-RQ through early fusion with a video model trained from scratch.
entries.condition: Related work on audio-only-to-AV adaptation [6,7].
entries.quote: FAVA [6] adapts BEST-RQ [22], an audio self-supervised model, through early fusion with a video model trained from scratch.

entries.text: Adaptive AV prepends Whisper with an audio-visual Transformer that outputs a de-noised spectrogram, without feeding visual features into Whisper directly.
entries.condition: Related work [7].

entries.text: Inserting the gated cross-attention layers into the encoder instead of the decoder performed significantly worse; other insertion orders inside the decoder block were slightly worse; no numbers are given for either.
entries.condition: Whisper-Medium ablation described in text only; Table 2 lists early fusion, late fusion and decoder gated cross-attention.
entries.quote: inserting them into the encoder, but the performance was significantly worse

entries.text: The authors describe the new layers as a large set of adaptors: removing them returns the audio-only Whisper weights.
entries.condition: Two-stage training; Whisper frozen in stage two.

entries.text: The paper states that Whisper-Flamingo significantly outperforms audio-only Whisper in noise.
entries.condition: Abstract/introduction wording; no statistical test reported (t51).
entries.quote: Flamingo significantly outperforms the audio-only Whisper

entries.text: The paper sets aside work that uses visual context from images or instructional videos, loosely synchronised with the audio, as separate research.
entries.condition: Refers to AVFormer [23] and prompting Whisper [24].

entries.text: TM-seq2seq attends to audio and video encodings with separate attention in every decoder layer (decoder-side cross-modal attention, trained from scratch).
entries.quote: In this variant, separate attention heads are used for attending on the video and audio embeddings.

entries.text: AVFormer keeps the ASR model (BEST-RQ Conformer, RNN-T) and the CLIP visual extractor frozen and trains only bottleneck adapters and a visual projection.
entries.quote: During training, we only tune these two sets of additional parameters, while both the ASR model and the visual feature extractor are frozen

entries.text: AVFormer injects projected full-frame CLIP features into the frozen ASR encoder; it does not use lip crops.
entries.quote: Unlike works that simply focus on lip mo- tion [1, 7, 23, 24, 29, 33, 37, 41], we investigate the contri- bution of entire visual frames.

entries.text: Prompting Whisper for AVSR feeds CLIP-retrieved object labels from full RGB frames into Whisper as a text prompt (zero-shot, VisSpeech).

MuAViC builds noisy translation tests by adding multilingual babble at 0 dB SNR to clean speech; En-X uses bilingual AV-HuBERT models, one per language pair. Per-pair fine-tuning is stated by the target (t76).

questions.q: Does adding visual features improve noisy English recognition over fine-tuned audio-only Whisper under the paper's matched LRS3 protocol?
questions.answer: In the reported LRS3 conditions, Whisper-Flamingo Large reduces noisy WER from 11.7% to 5.6%, while clean WER is 1.5% versus 2.3% for audio-only fine-tuned Whisper-Large. Cross-paper comparisons remain limited by differing babble files.

questions.q: Does the audio-visual system improve noisy En-X translation over its audio-only initialization, and how does it compare with the prior multilingual AV system?
questions.answer: On the reported MuAViC noisy evaluation, Whisper-Flamingo Large improves average BLEU from 18.6 to 20.5 and English WER from 13.8% to 7.2% versus audio-only Whisper-Large. Its average BLEU is slightly below Bilingual AV-HuBERT (20.5 versus 20.8), while it handles English transcription and six translation directions with one parameter set.

questions.q: How strong is the evidence for superiority over prior AVSR systems?
questions.answer: The paper reports comparable clean and slightly better noisy LRS3 results than AV-HuBERT, but u-HuBERT has the best reported noisy LRS3 WER and was not tested as a feature encoder. The authors explicitly caution that the noise files differ or were unavailable, and uncertainty estimates and significance tests are not reported.

questions.q: Which evaluation details omitted from the paper are material for interpreting reproducibility and test-set scope?
questions.answer: The code sets seed 3407, normalizes video pixels and waveform amplitudes, normalizes multilingual labels, and caps En-X validation/test lists at 200 examples per language. The paper does not report speaker/session overlap or MuAViC per-language test counts, and the training script also computes test metrics during validation cycles.

questions.q: Which papers decide the fusion and translation verdicts, and how do they inject visual information or produce translations? (reader, q1/answer.json)
questions.answer: See p1-p6: TM-seq2seq separate audio/video attention in the decoder; AVFormer frozen ASR + adapters + full-frame CLIP tokens in the encoder; prompting Whisper with CLIP labels; MuAViC bilingual AV-HuBERT per pair with 0 dB multilingual babble; MixSpeech visual-only translation on AVMuST-TED.

questions.q: Does the released code cap the reported En-X test sets at 200 examples per language (t55, t64)?
questions.answer: No. reduce_val=200 is passed only in the training script; whisper_decode_video.py:61 calls load_data without reduce_val, so the decoding test split is complete. t55 and t64 corrected (writer check of the public repository).
